questions.title: Antimycin and the electron transport chain
questions.question: Antimycin inhibits the electron transport chain at which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Complex I is blocked by rotenone, not antimycin — a different inhibitor entirely, at the entry point of the chain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is inhibited by malonate, and is bypassed by the FADH2 route rather than being antimycin's target.
explanations.C: Correct. Antimycin A binds cytochrome b within Complex III (ubiquinol–cytochrome c oxidoreductase) and blocks electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, halting oxidative phosphorylation at that specific point in the chain. This makes antimycin useful experimentally to isolate ETC segments proximal to Complex III from those distal to it when studying electron flow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) is the site blocked by cyanide and azide, the classic terminal-step poisons, not antimycin.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name Complex III as antimycin's site of block, distinct from the Complex I and Complex IV inhibitor sites.

questions.title: Substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle
questions.question: Substrate level phosphorylation is the process of phosphorylation at the level of the reaction itself. In the TCA cycle it occurs in which step?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Isocitrate dehydrogenase generates NADH for later oxidative phosphorylation; it does not phosphorylate a nucleotide directly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Malate dehydrogenase likewise yields NADH, not a directly phosphorylated nucleotide — it feeds the electron transport chain rather than performing substrate-level phosphorylation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aconitase catalyses an isomerisation (citrate to isocitrate) with no redox or phosphorylation event at all.
explanations.D: Correct. The succinyl-CoA synthetase (succinate thiokinase) step converts succinyl-CoA to succinate while generating GTP directly from the reaction's own energy — the one substrate-level phosphorylation event in the TCA cycle, readily converted to ATP. Because GTP is a high-energy phosphate compound interconvertible with ATP via nucleoside diphosphate kinase, this single step still contributes directly to the cell's usable energy pool.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify succinyl-CoA synthetase as the TCA-cycle step performing substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.title: Peroxidase enzyme mechanism
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true concerning the peroxidase enzyme?

options.A: It acts on two molecules of H2O2
options.B: It does not need the presence of a hydrogen donor
options.C: It interferes with chain propagation of free radicals
options.D: It prevents the process of initiation of free radicals

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acting on two molecules of H2O2 at once (2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2) describes catalase's dismutation reaction, not the peroxidase route, which reduces one H2O2 molecule using a hydrogen donor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is catalase that needs no hydrogen donor; peroxidase enzymes (such as glutathione peroxidase) specifically require a hydrogen donor — reduced glutathione — to reduce H2O2 to water.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chain propagation is the stage at which an existing free radical reacts further; enzymatic H2O2 removal acts earlier, before a radical chain has even started.
explanations.D: Correct. By removing hydrogen peroxide before it can generate hydroxyl radicals (via the iron-catalysed Fenton reaction), peroxidase activity prevents the initiation step of free-radical chain reactions rather than acting once radicals are already propagating. This is why maintaining catalase and glutathione peroxidase activity is protective against oxidative stress, rather than merely mopping up radicals after damage has already begun.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that peroxide-disposing enzymes act by preventing free-radical initiation, and correctly assign the no-hydrogen-donor/two-substrate-molecule facts to catalase rather than peroxidase.

questions.title: Thiamine-dependent enzyme for brain glucose oxidation
questions.question: A 55-year-old alcoholic was brought to the Emergency Department by his friends. The doctor ordered an injection of thiamine followed by overnight parenteral glucose. The next morning the patient was alert, serum thiamine was normal, and blood glucose was 73 mg/dL. Which of the following enzymes is thiamine-dependent and essential for glucose oxidation in the brain?

explanations.A: Correct. Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires thiamine pyrophosphate as one of its five coenzymes and is the irreversible, committed step linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle — the brain depends on it almost exclusively for oxidative glucose metabolism. This is exactly why thiamine is given before glucose in a suspected alcoholic: giving glucose first can consume the little thiamine reserve that remains and precipitate acute Wernicke's encephalopathy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Isocitrate dehydrogenase uses NAD+ (or NADP+ for the cytosolic isoform), not thiamine pyrophosphate, as its coenzyme.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Succinyl-CoA thiokinase (synthetase) uses GDP/GTP and CoA, not thiamine, in its substrate-level phosphorylation reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD, not thiamine pyrophosphate, and is also the enzyme complex that doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify pyruvate dehydrogenase as the thiamine-dependent enzyme essential for brain glucose oxidation, in the context of Wernicke's-risk thiamine-before-glucose management.

questions.title: Site of activity of the hexose monophosphate pathway
questions.question: The hexose monophosphate pathway (HMP) is an important pathway in glucose metabolism. Which of the following statements is true?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle has comparatively little HMP-pathway activity because it has low demand for NADPH-driven biosynthesis (fatty acid and steroid synthesis) compared with the tissues that do run this pathway heavily.
explanations.B: Correct. The hexose monophosphate pathway runs actively in the liver (along with adrenal cortex, adipose tissue, lactating mammary gland, testis and red cells) — tissues with a high demand for NADPH to drive fatty acid synthesis, steroidogenesis, and glutathione regeneration. This tissue distribution mirrors exactly where NADPH-dependent biosynthesis is most active, which is the physiological reason the pathway concentrates there rather than in tissues such as skeletal muscle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The HMP pathway does not generate ATP; its purpose is to generate NADPH (for reductive biosynthesis) and ribose 5-phosphate (for nucleotide synthesis), not energy in the form of ATP.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The HMP pathway is entirely cytosolic, not mitochondrial — this is part of what lets it run independently of the cell's mitochondrial oxidative state.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the HMP pathway is active in liver, cytosolic, and does not generate ATP.

questions.title: Key regulatory enzyme of haem synthesis
questions.question: What is the key regulatory enzyme in haemoglobin synthesis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Haem synthase" is not the pathway's rate-limiting step and is more properly the name occasionally used for ferrochelatase itself, the pathway's final enzyme rather than its regulatory one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ALA dehydratase performs the second step of the pathway (converting ALA to porphobilinogen); it is not the pathway's rate-limiting, regulated enzyme.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ferrochelatase catalyses the final step, inserting Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX — an essential step, but not the one haem itself feeds back on to control overall production.
explanations.D: Correct. ALA synthase, in the mitochondrion, condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA in the first and rate-limiting step of haem synthesis, and is the enzyme haem feeds back on (via negative feedback and repression of gene transcription) to switch production down when haem is abundant. Because it sits at this very first committed step, throttling ALA synthase is the most efficient point in the whole pathway for haem to regulate its own future production.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify ALA synthase as the rate-limiting, feedback-regulated enzyme of haem synthesis.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Haem synthesis

questions.title: Ammonia detoxification in the brain
questions.question: Ammonia (NH3) is detoxified in the brain in the form of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ornithine is a urea-cycle intermediate in the liver, not the form the brain uses to carry ammonia away safely.
explanations.B: Correct. The brain detoxifies ammonia by combining it with glutamate via glutamine synthetase to form glutamine — a non-toxic carrier that can leave the brain and be transported to the liver or kidney for further processing. This route matters clinically because impaired hepatic ammonia clearance lets blood ammonia rise and cross into the brain, where astrocytes convert it to glutamine at the cost of osmotic swelling that contributes to hepatic encephalopathy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Asparagine is formed similarly to glutamine (from aspartate) but is not the brain's principal ammonia-carrying molecule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alanine is the form muscle uses to export nitrogen (the glucose-alanine cycle), not the brain's own route, which relies on glutamine synthesis instead.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the brain detoxifies ammonia as glutamine, distinct from muscle's alanine route.

questions.title: Cytochrome P450 mechanism in phase 1 metabolism
questions.question: Which one of the following is correct about cytochrome P450 in phase 1 reactions of xenobiotic metabolism?

options.A: It acts only on exogenous compounds such as drugs
options.D: It is formed of 450 amino acids

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cytochrome P450 also hydroxylates endogenous substrates — steroids, fatty acids and bile acid precursors among them — it is not restricted to exogenous drugs and toxins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A di-oxygenase would incorporate both atoms of molecular oxygen into the substrate; cytochrome P450 incorporates only one, reducing the other to water.
explanations.C: Correct. Cytochrome P450 is a haem-containing monooxygenase (mixed function oxidase): it inserts one atom of molecular oxygen into the substrate as a hydroxyl group while reducing the second oxygen atom to water, using NADPH as the electron source. This single-oxygen-insertion mechanism is also what makes P450 activity inducible and inhibitable by other drugs, the molecular basis of many clinically important drug-drug interactions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "P450" names the 450 nm absorbance peak of its reduced, carbon-monoxide-bound form on a spectrophotometer, not an amino-acid count.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that cytochrome P450 acts as a monooxygenase, and correct the exogenous-only and di-oxygenase distractors.

questions.title: Starting materials of haem synthesis
questions.question: Along with succinyl-CoA, which of the following amino acids serves as starting material in haem synthesis?

explanations.A: Correct. ALA synthase condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the first and rate-limiting step of haem synthesis — glycine is the amino acid that donates the nitrogen and part of the carbon skeleton to the pathway. Losing either substrate stalls the pathway at its very first step, before any of the later cytosolic or mitochondrial intermediates can even form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysine is not a substrate of the haem-synthesis pathway; it is better known for its role in collagen cross-linking and carnitine synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Serine is not a haem-synthesis substrate, though it is a precursor for glycine itself via one-carbon metabolism — an indirect, not direct, relationship.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alanine feeds gluconeogenesis (via the glucose-alanine cycle) and transamination reactions, not haem synthesis.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name glycine as the amino acid that condenses with succinyl-CoA to start haem synthesis.

questions.title: Chymotrypsin's optimum pH, class and secreted form
questions.question: Which one of the following is correct about chymotrypsin?

options.C: It acts on peptide linkages between aromatic amino acids
options.D: It is secreted in active form

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin, like the other pancreatic proteases, has an alkaline (not acidic) pH optimum, matching the alkaline environment created by pancreatic bicarbonate secretion in the duodenum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin is an endopeptidase, cleaving bonds in the middle of the polypeptide chain — the exopeptidases (carboxypeptidase, aminopeptidase) trim single residues from the chain ends instead.
explanations.C: Correct. Chymotrypsin cleaves peptide bonds specifically on the carboxyl side of the bulky aromatic amino acids phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan. This bulky-side-chain specificity complements trypsin, which instead targets the smaller basic residues lysine and arginine, so that together the two enzymes cover a broad range of internal peptide bonds.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin, like trypsin, is secreted as the inactive zymogen chymotrypsinogen and requires proteolytic activation (by trypsin) before it becomes active — it is not secreted in active form.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Correctly assign chymotrypsin's pH optimum, endopeptidase class and zymogen activation, and its aromatic-residue specificity.

questions.title: Substrates excluded from gluconeogenesis
questions.question: Gluconeogenesis is the production of glucose from non-carbohydrate molecules. Which of the following is not a substrate for gluconeogenesis?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. it is a genuine substrate). Lactate is converted back to pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase and enters gluconeogenesis via the Cori cycle.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. it is a genuine substrate). Alanine is transaminated to pyruvate in the liver, feeding gluconeogenesis via the glucose-alanine cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. it is a genuine substrate). Glycerol, released from triacylglycerol hydrolysis, enters via dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
explanations.D: Correct. Acetyl-CoA cannot be a net substrate for gluconeogenesis in mammals — the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction producing it is irreversible, and the two carbons acetyl-CoA contributes to the TCA cycle are exactly balanced by two carbons lost as CO2 in one turn, leaving no net carbon skeleton available for glucose synthesis. This is exactly why a metabolic state that shunts carbon predominantly into acetyl-CoA, such as heavy fat oxidation, cannot by itself replenish blood glucose.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name acetyl-CoA as the substrate excluded from gluconeogenesis, and explain the carbon-balance reason.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Bioenergetics

questions.title: Glucokinase versus hexokinase
questions.question: The first step of glycolysis is conversion of glucose to glucose 6-phosphate by glucokinase. Which of the following is the true statement concerning glucokinase?

options.C: Has a higher Km for glucose than does hexokinase

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is hexokinase, not glucokinase, that is allosterically inhibited by its own product, glucose 6-phosphate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucokinase is restricted to liver and pancreatic beta cells; hexokinase, not glucokinase, is present in essentially all tissue cells, including muscle.
explanations.C: Correct. Glucokinase has a high Km for glucose (low affinity), which is exactly what lets it respond to the wide swings of glucose concentration seen after a meal — hexokinase, by contrast, has a low Km (high affinity) and stays near-saturated even at low glucose, guaranteeing baseline glucose uptake to every tissue. This kinetic difference is also why glucokinase, not hexokinase, is the glucose sensor that couples blood glucose level to insulin secretion in the pancreatic beta cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both hexokinase and glucokinase catalyse an essentially irreversible reaction (a large negative free-energy change), not a reversible one.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Contrast glucokinase and hexokinase by Km, tissue distribution and product inhibition.

questions.title: Enzyme inserting iron into protoporphyrin
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes catalyses the incorporation of the ferrous ion into protoporphyrin IX?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ferroxidase (caeruloplasmin's activity) oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+ for loading onto transferrin — a plasma iron-handling role, not haem synthesis.
explanations.B: Correct. Ferrochelatase, the final enzyme of haem synthesis, inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX to form haem — it is one of the two mitochondrial steps of the pathway (alongside ALA synthase), and is also one of the two enzymes lead inhibits in lead poisoning, alongside ALA dehydratase. Because ferrochelatase activity is blocked by lead, lead poisoning characteristically produces an anaemia with accumulated protoporphyrin and reduced haem output.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ferroreductase reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+, typically at the point of intestinal absorption or before mitochondrial uptake, rather than inserting iron into protoporphyrin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase acts earlier in the pathway, converting coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX — before iron is ever inserted.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name ferrochelatase as the enzyme inserting Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX to complete haem synthesis.

questions.title: Enzyme deficient in Von Gierke's disease
questions.question: Which one of the following enzymes is deficient in Von Gierke's disease?

explanations.A: Correct. Von Gierke's disease (glycogen storage disease type I) is caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; every clinical feature follows from glucose 6-phosphate that cannot be dephosphorylated and released as free glucose, producing severe fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly. Because both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis converge on glucose 6-phosphate before it can be released as free glucose, this single enzyme defect blocks the liver's two main routes of raising blood glucose at once.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alpha-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency causes Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II), a lysosomal storage disorder with cardiomyopathy, not Von Gierke's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alpha-1,6-glucosidase (debranching enzyme) deficiency causes Cori disease (glycogen storage disease type III), with a milder phenotype than Von Gierke's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Liver phosphorylase deficiency causes Hers disease (glycogen storage disease type VI), generally milder than glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency as the cause of Von Gierke's disease, distinct from the other glycogen storage diseases.

questions.title: Hormonal control of glycogen phosphorylase and synthase
questions.question: Epinephrine and glucagon have which one of the following effects on hepatic glycogen metabolism?

options.A: Both glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase are activated by phosphorylation but at significantly different rates
options.B: Glycogen phosphorylase is inactivated, whereas glycogen synthase is activated
options.C: Glycogen phosphorylase is phosphorylated and active, whereas glycogen synthase is phosphorylated and inactive
options.D: The net synthesis of glycogen is increased

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phosphorylation does not activate both enzymes — it activates glycogen phosphorylase but inactivates glycogen synthase, a reciprocal (not uniform) effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the actual effect: epinephrine and glucagon phosphorylate and activate glycogen phosphorylase, not inactivate it.
explanations.C: Correct. Epinephrine and glucagon raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A, which phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase into its active form (driving glycogenolysis) and glycogen synthase into its inactive form (shutting off glycogen synthesis) at the same time — reciprocal regulation that switches net glycogen flux cleanly in one direction. This design is efficient because it avoids the wasted energy of running glycogen breakdown and synthesis simultaneously, a phenomenon sometimes called a futile cycle if left unchecked.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Net glycogen synthesis falls, not rises, under these hormones — they mobilise glucose from glycogen stores rather than building them up.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that epinephrine/glucagon phosphorylate glycogen phosphorylase to active and glycogen synthase to inactive at the same time, and reject the uniform-activation and increased-synthesis distractors.

questions.title: Source of free glucose during glycogenolysis
questions.question: Glycogenolysis is the main source of blood glucose during fasting for less than 18 hours. During glycogenolysis, free glucose is produced by which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose 1-phosphate (not free glucose) from the outer branches of glycogen, and it also stalls four residues short of each branch point.
explanations.B: Correct. Debranching enzyme completes what phosphorylase cannot: after phosphorylase strips the outer chain down to four residues from a branch point, debranching enzyme transfers three residues to a nearby chain and then hydrolyses the single remaining alpha-1,6-linked glucose, releasing it as free glucose (not glucose 1-phosphate). A deficiency of this enzyme (Cori disease) leaves a glycogen molecule with only its outer branches trimmed to short stubs, producing a milder hypoglycaemic phenotype than the complete block seen in Von Gierke's disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Branching enzyme acts during glycogen synthesis, not breakdown, creating alpha-1,6 branch points rather than removing them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Phosphatase" alone is not the named enzyme of this step; the specific enzyme is debranching enzyme's hydrolase activity, not a generic phosphatase.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify debranching enzyme as the source of free glucose (not glucose 1-phosphate) during glycogenolysis.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Glycogen storage disease

questions.title: Character of the glutamate dehydrogenase deamination reaction
questions.question: L-Glutamate dehydrogenase is an enzyme for the deamination reaction. Which of the following is a character of this reaction?

options.B: Needs NADP or NADPH as coenzymes

explanations.A: Correct. Glutamate dehydrogenase oxidatively deaminates glutamate to produce free ammonia and alpha-ketoglutarate, the reaction that funnels amino groups collected from transamination reactions into free ammonia for urea synthesis. This reaction is the key point where the amino groups collected from many different amino acids are finally released as free ammonia for entry into the urea cycle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glutamate dehydrogenase is unusual in accepting either NAD+ or NADP+ as its coenzyme, not needing the reduced forms NADH/NADPH — the reaction runs in the oxidative (deaminating) direction using the oxidised coenzyme.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The glutamate dehydrogenase reaction is reversible, running in either the deaminating (glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate) or aminating direction depending on cellular conditions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. FMN is not this enzyme's coenzyme; glutamate dehydrogenase uses NAD+/NADP+, not a flavin coenzyme.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that glutamate dehydrogenase's deamination produces ammonia and alpha-ketoglutarate, and correct the coenzyme and reversibility distractors.

questions.title: Rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle
questions.question: Which one of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme in the urea cycle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. N-acetylglutamate synthase makes the allosteric activator (N-acetylglutamate) that commits the true rate-limiting enzyme, but is not itself the rate-limiting step.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Argininosuccinate synthase catalyses a later cytosolic step (combining citrulline and aspartate) — an important control point in some contexts, but not the pathway's overall rate-limiting enzyme.
explanations.C: Correct. Carbamoyl phosphate synthase I, the first and mitochondrial step of the urea cycle, is rate-limiting and is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate — the committed step that determines the overall pace of urea production. Because N-acetylglutamate is itself made from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by a reaction stimulated by arginine, this arrangement links urea-cycle activity to the amount of amino-acid nitrogen actually available for disposal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Argininosuccinate lyase splits argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate, a downstream cytosolic step, not the pathway's rate-limiting enzyme.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify carbamoyl phosphate synthase I as the rate-limiting, N-acetylglutamate-activated enzyme of the urea cycle.

questions.title: Lipoprotein lipase characteristics
questions.question: Lipoprotein lipase, secreted post-prandially, helps digest lipids. This enzyme is characterised by which of the following?

options.B: Is present in the cytosol of adipocytes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triacylglycerol, not cholesteryl esters — cholesteryl ester hydrolysis is handled by different enzymes (such as hormone-sensitive lipase's cholesteryl esterase activity or lysosomal acid lipase).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lipoprotein lipase is anchored to the luminal surface of capillary endothelium (via heparan sulphate proteoglycans), not sitting free in the adipocyte cytosol.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Insulin induces (up-regulates) lipoprotein lipase, particularly in adipose tissue after a meal — it does not inhibit it.
explanations.D: Correct. Lipoprotein lipase, anchored at the capillary wall and activated by apolipoprotein C-II, hydrolyses the triacylglycerol carried in chylomicrons (and VLDL), releasing fatty acids for tissue uptake. This same enzyme, expressed differently across tissues, is why the fed state's insulin favours fat storage in adipose tissue while fasting instead favours fatty-acid delivery to muscle.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses TAG in chylomicrons at the capillary wall, and correct the location, substrate and insulin-effect distractors.

questions.title: Pepsinogen secretion and activation
questions.question: Regarding pepsinogens, which of the following statements is appropriate?

options.C: Their secretion is linked with HCl secretion

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pepsin (from pepsinogen) digests protein, not carbohydrate — carbohydrate digestion is handled by amylases, not gastric proteases.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pepsinogen is secreted by chief (zymogenic) cells, not parietal cells — parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor instead.
explanations.C: Correct. Chief-cell pepsinogen secretion and parietal-cell HCl secretion are functionally linked: HCl is what converts pepsinogen to active pepsin, and pepsin then autocatalytically activates further pepsinogen molecules, so the two secretory processes work together as one digestive step. This coupling means any condition that impairs acid secretion, such as achlorhydria, also blunts pepsin-mediated protein digestion even though pepsinogen itself is still being secreted normally.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pepsin's optimum pH is strongly acidic, around 1.5-2.5 (reflecting the stomach's own acidity), not the 4-5.3 range given here.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that pepsinogen secretion and activation are linked to HCl secretion, and correct the cell-source, digestive-target and pH distractors.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

questions.title: Inhibitor of gastrin secretion
questions.question: Regarding gastrin hormone secretion, which of the following inhibits it?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Caffeine stimulates gastric acid secretion directly (via a gastrin-independent, adenosine-receptor-mediated route), it does not inhibit gastrin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gastric distension stimulates gastrin release (part of the gastric phase of secretion), the opposite of inhibition.
explanations.C: Correct. Somatostatin, released by antral D cells when the antrum becomes acidic, inhibits gastrin secretion from G cells — a negative-feedback loop that limits further acid output once the stomach is already acidic. This loop is the physiological target of somatostatin analogues such as octreotide, used clinically to suppress pathological gastrin-driven acid hypersecretion in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Protein digestion products (peptides, amino acids) are classic stimulants of gastrin release, not inhibitors.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify somatostatin as the inhibitor of gastrin secretion among stimulatory distractors.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

field_notes.keySource: hand-drawn-ink key, corrupted glyph on option c, confirmed by render --force (coverage/ZU-MED-107-triage.md)

questions.title: Factors relaxing the ileocecal sphincter
questions.question: Concerning the ileocecal sphincter, it is relaxed by all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. gastrin does relax it). Gastrin, released as part of the gastroileal reflex when food enters the stomach, promotes relaxation of the ileocecal sphincter to allow ileal contents through.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. ileal distension does relax it). Distension of the ileum itself promotes relaxation of the sphincter, allowing forward flow of chyme into the caecum.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. gastric distension does relax it). Gastric distension, via the gastroileal reflex, also promotes ileocecal sphincter relaxation.
explanations.D: Correct — this is the exception. Over-distension of the caecum has the opposite effect: it triggers reflex contraction (closure) of the ileocecal sphincter, preventing further filling and backflow of caecal contents into the ileum, rather than relaxing it. This directional control — relax on the proximal side, close on the distal side — coordinates one-way forward flow of chyme while guarding against caecal reflux, rather than simply reacting to any nearby stretch.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify caecal over-distension as the factor that closes (not relaxes) the ileocecal sphincter, opposite to ileal/gastric distension and gastrin.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

questions.title: Trigger of reflex vomiting
questions.question: Reflex vomiting is produced by which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect (a real but different mechanism). Vomiting of early pregnancy is driven mainly by rising hCG/oestrogen and vestibular sensitivity, a hormonal route rather than a direct mucosal reflex.
explanations.B: Correct. Irritation of the gastric mucosa — by infection, toxins or chemical irritants — activates visceral afferents that trigger the vomiting reflex directly, the classic "reflex" vomiting mechanism this question is naming. Recognising a direct mucosal trigger rather than a centrally mediated one matters clinically, since the two routes often call for different management even though both end in the same vomiting reflex arc.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a real but different mechanism). Vomiting in diabetic ketoacidosis is driven by acidosis and ketone-body stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone, a centrally mediated metabolic route rather than a direct mucosal reflex.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a real but different mechanism). Vomiting in renal failure is driven by accumulated uraemic toxins acting on the chemoreceptor trigger zone, again a centrally mediated toxin route rather than a direct mucosal reflex.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify gastric mucosal irritation as a direct reflex trigger for vomiting, distinct from the hormonal/metabolic/toxin-mediated causes listed as distractors.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

questions.title: Biochemical picture of post-hepatic jaundice
questions.question: In post-hepatic jaundice, which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Van den Bergh test is direct

explanations.A: Correct. Post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice results from blocked bile flow after conjugation, so conjugated (water-soluble, direct-reacting) bilirubin accumulates in blood and gives a direct van den Bergh reaction. Recognising this whole pattern together — not any single feature alone — is what lets a clinician distinguish obstructive jaundice from pre-hepatic (unconjugated, normal stool/urine) and hepatic jaundice at the bedside.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut in obstructive jaundice, urobilinogen formation falls, not rises.
explanations.C: Incorrect. With little or no bilirubin reaching the gut, stool becomes pale/clay-coloured, not darker than normal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and is excreted in urine when it backs up into blood, so urine darkens rather than staying normal.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that post-hepatic jaundice gives a direct van den Bergh reaction, falling urobilinogen, pale stool and dark urine.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

questions.title: Vagal stimulation of gastric secretion by hypoglycaemia
questions.question: Concerning gastric secretion, which of the following is true?

options.A: Hyperosmotic diet in the duodenum increases gastric secretion
options.B: Enterogastric hormones increase emptying of the stomach
options.C: Hypoglycaemia stimulates secretion via a vagal reflex
options.D: The sham feeding experiment proves the gastric phase of secretion

explanations.A: Incorrect. A hyperosmotic duodenal diet triggers the enterogastric reflex, which inhibits (not increases) gastric secretion and emptying.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Enterogastric hormones (secretin, GIP, CCK) inhibit gastric emptying, they do not increase it.
explanations.C: Correct. Hypoglycaemia is sensed centrally and stimulates gastric acid secretion through a vagal reflex, independent of food actually being in the stomach — the same reflex arc exploited clinically by the insulin (hypoglycaemia) test of vagal completeness after vagotomy. This same vagal pathway is deliberately tested with that insulin test, used after peptic ulcer surgery to confirm that a vagotomy was truly complete.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sham feeding is the classic experiment proving the cephalic phase of gastric secretion, not the gastric phase (which is instead demonstrated by direct gastric distension/protein-product experiments).

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that hypoglycaemia stimulates gastric secretion via a vagal reflex, and correct the enterogastric-inhibition and sham-feeding/cephalic-phase distractors.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

questions.title: Stimulant of gallbladder contractility
questions.question: Regarding gallbladder contractility, which one of the following stimulates it?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atropine, an anticholinergic, blocks parasympathetic (vagal) input to the gallbladder and relaxes it, rather than stimulating contraction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation relaxes the gallbladder (and constricts the sphincter of Oddi), a "rest and digest"-opposing effect, not a contractile one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secretin acts mainly on pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, not primarily on gallbladder contraction — CCK is the dominant biliary-contraction hormone.
explanations.D: Correct. CCK, released from duodenal mucosa in response to fat and protein digestion products, contracts the gallbladder wall and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi together, delivering bile into the duodenum when it is needed for fat digestion. This coordinated relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi alongside gallbladder contraction lets bile flow into the duodenum precisely when a fatty meal needs it, rather than continuously.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify CCK as the hormone that stimulates gallbladder contraction, distinct from atropine and sympathetic relaxation and from secretin's separate pancreatic role.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Biliary physiology

questions.title: Factor increasing exocrine pancreatic secretion
questions.question: As regards control of pancreatic secretion, which of the following factors increases the secretion of the exocrine pancreas?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atropine blocks the vagally mediated (cholinergic) component of pancreatic acinar secretion, reducing rather than increasing pancreatic output.
explanations.B: Correct. Secretin, released from duodenal S cells in response to acid chyme, stimulates a high-volume, bicarbonate-rich pancreatic ductal secretion — the major hormonal driver of exocrine pancreatic output, further augmented by CCK. CCK then augments this secretin-driven ductal secretion, so the two hormones work together rather than through entirely separate mechanisms to match pancreatic output to the meal actually eaten.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation generally inhibits, rather than increases, glandular secretion including pancreatic exocrine output.
explanations.D: Incorrect. VIP has some secretory effects at other sites, but it is not the principal stimulant of exocrine pancreatic secretion tested here — secretin holds that role.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify secretin as the hormone that increases exocrine pancreatic secretion, among inhibitory or unrelated distractors.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Pancreatic secretion

questions.title: A genuine function of the stomach
questions.question: The stomach has many functions. Which of the following is one of them?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stomach absorbs only a small fraction of ingested water; most water absorption occurs in the small intestine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the stomach — though gastric acid does help convert dietary iron to its more absorbable ferrous form.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The stomach only partially digests protein, via pepsin; complete protein digestion requires the pancreatic and brush-border enzymes further down the tract.
explanations.D: Correct. One of the stomach's core functions is to act as a reservoir, storing a meal and releasing it into the duodenum gradually rather than all at once, matching the duodenum's limited processing capacity. This reservoir role is also why gastric surgery that removes or bypasses this storage capacity, as in gastrectomy, can produce dumping syndrome, when a meal empties into the small intestine far faster than it should.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify storage of food as a genuine gastric function, and reject the overstated water-absorption, iron-absorption and complete-protein-digestion distractors.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

questions.title: A function of gastric HCl
questions.question: HCl is secreted by the oxyntic (parietal) cells of the stomach. Which one of the following is a function of HCl?

explanations.A: Incorrect. HCl activates pepsinogen to pepsin; trypsinogen is instead activated by enteropeptidase (enterokinase) in the duodenum, not by gastric HCl.
explanations.B: Incorrect. HCl has no fat-absorption role — fat digestion and absorption depend on bile salts, pancreatic lipase and the small intestinal mucosa, downstream of the stomach.
explanations.C: Correct. Gastric HCl provides a bactericidal barrier, killing most ingested bacteria before they can reach and colonise the small intestine — a genuine, independent function distinct from its role in pepsinogen activation. This is also why long-term acid suppression, whether from disease or from acid-suppressing drugs, is associated with a modestly increased risk of enteric infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. HCl denatures/unfolds dietary protein to expose it to pepsin, and it does not itself absorb protein — protein absorption occurs later, in the small intestine, after full digestion to amino acids and small peptides.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify killing ingested bacteria as a genuine, independent function of gastric HCl, distinct from its role in pepsinogen activation.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric secretion

questions.title: Structure compressed by a pancreatic neck cyst
questions.question: A 55-year-old man was admitted to hospital with acute abdomen; investigation revealed a cyst in the neck of the pancreas. Which of the following could be compressed directly by that cyst?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The left gastric vein drains toward the portal vein but does not sit directly posterior to the pancreatic neck in the same way the portal vein's point of formation does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior mesenteric artery is not in direct relation to the pancreatic neck; it lies more caudally, related to the left colon and rectum.
explanations.C: Correct. The neck of the pancreas lies directly anterior to the point where the splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein — a cyst or mass at the pancreatic neck can therefore compress the portal vein directly, a clinically important relation in staging pancreatic disease. This relation is why imaging staging of a pancreatic neck mass specifically looks for portal vein involvement, since that finding can change whether the tumour is considered resectable.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior pancreaticoduodenal vein relates to the pancreatic head, not the neck, and drains into the portal vein rather than being the structure directly compressed at the neck.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify the portal vein as the structure directly related to (and compressible by) the neck of the pancreas.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Pancreas anatomy

questions.title: Structure related to the quadrate lobe of the liver
questions.question: A 76-year-old man underwent hepatic surgery. During the operation, the surgeon injured a structure related to the quadrate lobe of the liver. Which of the following could be the injured structure?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right kidney relates to the right lobe proper of the liver, not specifically to the quadrate lobe.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The right suprarenal gland likewise relates to the bare area/right lobe of the liver, not the quadrate lobe.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The right colic (hepatic) flexure relates to the right lobe's visceral surface near the gallbladder fossa's lateral aspect, but the specific structure paired with the quadrate lobe in this bank is the transverse colon.
explanations.D: Correct. The quadrate lobe sits on the liver's visceral surface, bounded by the gallbladder fossa, the fissure for the ligamentum teres and the porta hepatis — the transverse colon is the structure related to this specific region, at risk during surgery there. Surgeons operating in this specific region of the liver must therefore keep the transverse colon's course in mind, distinct from the separate set of structures at risk when operating nearer the right lobe proper.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify the transverse colon as the structure related to the quadrate lobe of the liver, distinct from the right kidney, suprarenal gland and colic flexure relations of the right lobe proper.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Pancreas anatomy

questions.title: Surface marking of the gallbladder fundus
questions.question: The fundus of the gallbladder lies at the tip of which of the following costal cartilages?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 7th costal cartilage is not the gallbladder fundus's landmark; it marks a different point along the costal margin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The 8th costal cartilage is likewise not the correct landmark for this surface marking.
explanations.C: Correct. The fundus of the gallbladder projects from beneath the liver's inferior border at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, at the point where the linea semilunaris crosses the costal margin — the anatomical basis of Murphy's point used clinically to examine for acute cholecystitis. This fixed surface projection is why Murphy's sign is elicited by palpating specifically at this point while asking the patient to inspire, rather than at an arbitrary point on the right upper quadrant.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 10th costal cartilage is not the gallbladder fundus's landmark; it lies further along the costal margin than the correct point.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State the 9th costal cartilage as the surface-anatomy landmark for the gallbladder fundus.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Pancreas anatomy

questions.title: Liver cell that stores vitamin A
questions.question: Which of the following cells in the liver stores vitamin A?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endothelial cells line the hepatic sinusoids; they do not store vitamin A.
explanations.B: Correct. Ito cells (hepatic stellate cells, fat-storing cells) sit in the space of Disse between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium and store the majority of the body's vitamin A as retinyl ester droplets — they are also the cells that activate into a collagen-producing, myofibroblast-like phenotype in liver fibrosis. This same cell type is clinically important well beyond its normal storage role, since its activation is the central cellular event driving progressive liver fibrosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Kupffer cells are the liver's resident macrophages, phagocytosing debris and old red cells; they do not store vitamin A.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cholangiocytes line the bile ducts and modify bile composition; they play no role in vitamin A storage.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify Ito cells as the vitamin A-storing cell type of the liver, distinct from endothelial cells, Kupffer cells and cholangiocytes.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Liver histology

field_notes.keySource: hand-drawn-ink key, corrupted glyph on option b, confirmed by render --force (coverage/ZU-MED-107-triage.md)

questions.title: Gastric cell type with zymogen granules
questions.question: Which of the following cells is characterised by the presence of zymogen granules?

explanations.A: Correct. Chief (zymogenic) cells, found mainly at the base of the gastric glands, are packed with apical zymogen granules containing pepsinogen and gastric lipase — this granular, secretory ultrastructure is their identifying histological feature. Because these granules store the inactive precursor pepsinogen rather than active pepsin, the cell protects itself from autodigestion until the granules' contents are secreted and activated by gastric acid outside the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Parietal cells are instead identified by an extensive intracellular canalicular system and abundant mitochondria, not zymogen granules.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mucous (neck) cells are identified by apical mucinogen droplets, a different secretory ultrastructure from zymogen granules.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enteroendocrine cells are identified by small basal secretory granules, positioned toward the base rather than the apex, and are not called zymogen granules.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify chief cells as the gastric cell type marked by apical zymogen granules, distinct from parietal, mucous neck and enteroendocrine cells.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Liver histology

questions.title: Distribution and features of fungiform papillae
questions.question: Regarding lingual papillae, which of the following characterises fungiform papillae?

options.A: Covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
options.B: Have numerous taste buds on their upper surfaces
options.C: The most numerous type of papillae in number
options.D: Scattered especially at the tip of the tongue

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fungiform papillae are covered by non-keratinised epithelium; keratinised stratified squamous epithelium instead covers filiform papillae.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fungiform papillae have relatively few taste buds on their upper surfaces; it is circumvallate papillae that carry numerous taste buds.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Filiform papillae are the most numerous type overall; fungiform papillae are comparatively fewer and scattered.
explanations.D: Correct. Fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped and scattered especially at the tip and lateral margins of the tongue, in contrast to the V-shaped row of circumvallate papillae at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third. This distribution and structure are why conditions that flatten the tongue's papillae, such as some nutritional deficiency states, blunt taste sensation disproportionately at the tip where fungiform papillae concentrate.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that fungiform papillae are scattered especially at the tongue's tip, non-keratinised, with relatively few taste buds, distinct from circumvallate and filiform papillae.
